made available to the nrovinces for educational purposes, "without encroaching in any way on the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in this field".
Well, I want to try to show hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that this is precisely what these agreements have done; and I should first like to give as an example the experience of my own province of Manitoba. The Manitoba revenues which were surrendered under these agreements in 1946 were worth a little over $8 million a year. In place of these we got under the agreement a guaranteed minimum of $13,500,000 and received in the year ended March 31, 1948, about $14,500,000. To make a long story short, Mr. Speaker, we shall receive in the present fiscal year, I believe-I have not checked the exact figure-something close to $35 million, which is more than our entire budget in 1949. Now, will any member of any party in this house have the hardihood to rise in his place and say that with this increase in revenue it is not possible for the provinces to support primary education?
What is your surplus this year?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What is the increase in the cost of education?
What was the federal budget in 1939?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let us leave that one province out. It is true Manitoba had a very favourable settlement in that contract, but let us take the agreement as a whole.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question before he leaves Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, surely.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the minister say whether he thinks the contributions made by the federal government to Manitoba for education, such as contributions for vocational training, contributions for the building of Carpathia school in Winnipeg and the school at Fort Churchill, all of which are outside of these grants, violate the Rowell-Sirois principle or interfere with provincial control over education?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I do not for one moment, because they are all earmarked grants, all made upon certain conditions which must be complied with; but they relate only to certain technical training.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I put it this way so as not to waste time. They do not relate to primary education.

Education

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Carpathia school is an
elementary school in the city of Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The school at Fort
Churchill is an elementary and high school.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: And it has nothing to do with primary education in general.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It certainly does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend cannot use up my time and trap me by these-
May I ask one question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
One at a time. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre cannot trap me by these atypical cases which he cites. He knows as perfectly well as I do that there is not now, in Canada, federal contributions to primary education, in the terms in which they are recommended in the resolution which is before us.
Now, let us take the grants from the federal treasury under these federal-provincial agreements. To go to the first post-war tax agreement, that is the first tax rental agreement in 1947-48, the sum of $80 million in that year was paid to seven provinces. In the last year of that same agreement 1951-52 another province having come in in the meantime, the $80 million had gone up to $122 million. Then a new agreement was negotiated, and in 1952-53 the first year of the new agreement with nine provinces that $80 million had gone up to $286 million, and in 1953-54 the second year of the second agreement, just one year later, it had gone up to $309 million by operation of the escalator clause, in order to take care of increased expenditures, including education. In 1956-57 the last year of that agreement, still with nine provinces, it had gone up by escalation and the like to $357 million.
Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No; my time is running out. I will be glad to answer the hon. member's questions at the end, if I have time.
During the past year we have been negotiating a third agreement, and we hope to have all the provinces of Canada included. The amount payable, as nearly as we can estimate it at this moment, under the third agreement is $640 million, plus certain other adjustments of taxation and so forth of $35 million, or a total of $675 million.
In other words the contribution of the federal government under this head in the period from 1947-48, when it was $80 million, has gone up in ten years to $675 million in 1957-58, or by almost eight and a half times.

Will any reasonable man tell me that in that large increase there is not elbow room within which the province of Alberta can find some way of taking care of its primary education, or even the province of Newfoundland? It is an increase of eight and a half times in federal payments.
The great virtue, Mr. Speaker, of this arrangement is that it complies with the resolution of my hon. friend from Saskatoon. This is the only way in which this money can be paid "without encroaching in any way upon the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces". As the provinces get this money, they can spend it on roads, they can spend it on bridges, they can spend it on graft, they can do what they like with it, or they can spend it on education.

Is the minister aware that one of his colleagues took the exactly opposite position in opposing this resolution? The Minister of National Health and Welfare said the reason it was unconstitutional was that it was earmarked for education.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I heard my colleague and I heard my hon. friend from Saskatoon. I think the explanation of my hon. friend's remark is that he himself did not understand the minister.
Thank you very much; no one else does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The fact of the matter is that the Rowell-Sirois commission was in my opinion much the most distinguished commission we had ever had. It would be a very happy situation if all our commissions produced as satisfactory a report as it did.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You had better explain yourself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And I would say that, because we have for our measures support from the fact that we took the Rowell-Sirois recommendations and implemented them. By and large, having regard to the fact that we have been passing through an era which has tested the financial arrangements of governments at every level, municipal, provincial and federal, the Rowell-Sirois policies have worked out remarkably well. They certainly have provided, if the provinces choose to spend it for that purpose, plenty of money with which to pay for education.
The hon. member for Saskatoon may perhaps recall that on an earlier occasion, I think it was in 1952, I pointed out that under these tax agreements then in effect over a period of five years not one of the treasuries of all the provinces of Canada had shown a deficit; they all showed surpluses, and those surpluses for the 5-year period totalled

nearly two-thirds of a billion dollars of provincial debt reduction. My hon. friend the hon. member for Saskatoon says, "If we do not pay some money they are going to have to close up primary education." Well, the only thing wrong with all these arguments is that the facts do not bear them out. It is only by ignoring the facts-I will not say suppressing them

but by paying no attention to them, that my hon. friend can make the kind of argument he does.
I sympathize entirely with him on the importance of primary education and the importance of increasing school teachers' salaries. But I say when he is proposing to do this by transgressing the provision which was put into the constitution of Canada most deliberately by the fathers of confederation, and which has proven over the years since to have been a very wise provision; and since the facts as I have related them show that the provinces, if they wish to do so, can make adequate provision for education, there is no case upon which he can ask for the support of his present resolution in this house.

Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to hear that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) had great sympathy for the hon. member for Saskatoon and for the position he took. I think it is unfortunate that the minister does not have a little knowledge as well about the real situation in the educational system, because I am quite sure there is not a teacher in the country who would not get up and refute everything he said. When he tells us and asks us to believe that the provinces are able to cope with this problem under the present financial arrangements, he flies right in the face of the express views of all educational authorities in Canada. The minister may be an expert in law, but I suspect he has not been paying very much attention to the mundane business of the local administration of schools or he would not attempt to put over as logical arguments the fantastic statements he has made this evening.
I was interested to find that apparently he bases his opposition to this resolution on two grounds. The first is the findings of the Rowell-Sirois commission. I remember the findings of that commission very well. I was a member of the British Columbia legislature at the time and it was notorious, as the Minister of Justice well knows, why that particular section of the Rowell-Sirois commission's report was included and why it contained the weak, feeble and unconvincing arguments he has quoted here tonight. At that time there was no doubt in the mind
Education
of anyone that it was a political consideration which forced that particular section of the Rowell-Sirois report.
The other ground upon which the minister apparently bases his position is a constitutional one, and I was quite interested when he suggested that of course there had been no contravention of provincial autonomy over education in regard to grants for universities, because they were all minor in quantity. I was reminded, Mr. Speaker, of the story you may remember about the young lady who was the subject of some censure over the results of her behaviour. Her defence was, "Well, it was such a very small baby". Surely, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice is the last person who should suggest to us that a minor fracture of the constitution is permissible but a large one is unthinkable.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He got away with a fairly large one.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: This resolution calls for payments to the provinces, if I read it correctly.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Surely these university
grants are not paid to the provinces. There is no parallel at all.

No, they are not paid to the provinces; and that brings me to another statement of the Minister of Justice when he suggested, if you please, Mr. Speaker, that provincial universities- and this is true of all the western universities -which have been established by provincial legislatures are more autonomous bodies than are provincial governments. What an astonishing point of view. We can make grants to universities because they are autonomous-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My hon. friend has attributed to me a suggestion which I did not make. He is confusing it with an inference which he improperly drew.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We all heard it.
Those were the words the minister used.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hansard will show the words I used.

Yes; if you do not change them, Hansard will show that you referred to universities as autonomous bodies, and therefore that the grants to them could not be put on the same basis as grants to provincial governments.

Education
Word for word.

I suggest to you, sir, that not only is the minister advancing quite a ridiculous argument, but he is also overlooking a very important factor. That is that provincial universities, while every effort has been made to remove them from the control of provincial governments, are nevertheless subject to considerable pressure when a provincial government wishes to exercise it, because the provincial government has control of all the grants. These arguments do not seem to add up to any sort of reality.
I want to deal particularly with the main thesis of the minister's refutation of the resolution tonight, and that is that the educational wants of Canadian children are or can be adequately cared for by the present fiscal arrangements. I want to suggest to him that his thinking is far out of date, because there is not a province in Canada at the present time that has established an adequate primary and secondary educational system.
I suppose sometimes we tend to forget what a very large bite we undertook to chew when in Canada we decided to educate all children, and we may also tend to forget that it is a relatively new development. It was a new idea when about 100 years ago, I suppose, perhaps a little more in some parts, it was decided to provide elementary education for all children. At that time it was possibly a fairly easily achieved ambition, because no doubt the first thought was that it would be very elementary education that the vast majority would require or would wish or would have to have provided for them. In fact until comparatively recent times this was the case.
I recall that when I went to high school in British Columbia a much smaller proportion of the children who attended elementary school with me went on to high school than today go from high school to university. At that time the high school student was the rarity, and the cost of education per capita was in consequence very much less than it is today. But I think we have to go even further than that. I think we must consider for a moment just what are the purposes of our education. Sometimes I am rather dismayed at the implications of some statements which are made with regard to education; the idea that the purpose of education is to produce so many people skilled in this particular line and so many in another specialized field and so many in some profession or trade. I think we lose sight of the fact that education is something else again. Education should primarily be the 
process of developing human beings, and in order to do that there is one thing we have to do which our educational system has never been able to do even from the start; that is to maintain and encourage the natural curiosity and inquisitiveness of the human being.
Every human being starts off life as a bundle of curiosity, and it is the way in which human beings develop and the way in which societies develop; but when you gather 40 or 50 pupils into a class and ask a teacher to take charge of them, all that teacher can do is to maintain sufficient order to wrest from those students an unwilling acceptance of certain information and facts. I have no doubt whatever that much of our trouble today with regard to juvenile delinquency has been primarily caused by the fact that our educational system stifles that necessary inquisitive, curious feature of human nature. In order to maintain it, the very first thing we need is about twice as many teachers as we have at the present time, and that is an extremely conservative estimate.
I would go further and quote something I said to a teachers' gathering in my constituency not long ago, when I told them- and you may think it was a very rash thing for a politician to say-that I hoped the time would come when half those in attendance at the gathering would be found unqualified for their jobs; but of course I was quite safe, because each one was quite convinced that I was referring to his neighbour and not to him. I then went on and suggested something further. I said I also hoped that I would see the status and the rewards of the teaching profession raised to the degree where there would be two applicants for every vacancy in the profession.
Unless we can approach something like that, then we are not going to really fulfil the fundamental purposes which were referred to tonight by the Minister of Justice, the purposes of the fathers of confederation, and so on. Today the world is a much more complex place than it was in their day. If ever there was a time when children required individual attention, when they required the encouragement of their speculative intellects, today is the time; because they have to combat an enormous barrage of influences and of propaganda which are definitely antisocial and anti-intellectual in nature.
We may think we can solve these problems by banning certain deleterious aspects of our society, like crime comics, but the only real protection for young people from some of the evil influences of modern society is the development in them of inquiring minds which will seek always to extend the boundaries of

Education
their knowledge. I suggest that in order to do this a very large proportion of the national income of this country must be devoted to providing the sort of scholastic environment which will produce those inquiring minds which will be made safe from the influences of some aspects of this modern world. To do that is beyond the capacity of even the richest province.
When the tax rental agreements were brought up in the legislature in Victoria I was very dubious about them. Curiously enough a Liberal member of the legislature and I were the only ones who were dubious. I was dubious because I doubted whether the great and good federal government would always see eye to eye with those of us who considered that there were vast improvements to be made in the society in which we lived. Tonight we have had proof that I was right. The spokesman for this government still does not admit that we have a crisis in education. Putting it in simple emotional terms, you may say that you cannot buy these things; but the bitter truth is that you have to buy them, and with hard dollars. We will have to offer inducements to the best brains in our society to undertake this most important job in our whole society, because the whole rest of our lives depends upon what those to whom we entrust our children are able to do with their trust.
The whole of our elaborate and complex society rests finally on the shoulders of the primary teacher. She is the first one who sets the child's mind in a certain direction. I would suggest that all the obstacles that have been raised tonight of insurmountable constitutional blocks will eventually be blown apart when finally it dawns on this government that it has to take action in this field, just as it took action in the field of family allowances, in the field of grants to universities, both of which I suggest are perhaps suspect to the constitutional purist. I have never been able to understand why grants in aid of technical education were not subject to the ban, but apparently they are not.
We know quite well that eventually, when they are met with the demands of public opinion, these blocks will be removed; but the tragic thing is that in the meantime a whole generation of Canadian citizens is suffering and much of the future of this country is being endangered, because if we go on this way we shall invite the worst possible fate that could overtake us. That is, that the next generation will be no wiser than we are.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, in the first place I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) on moving this resolution designed to give financial assistance to our educational institutions and teaching establishments. In so doing, he affords us all, as members of this house, an opportunity to show our interest in matters of education in this country. It is a valuable contribution to the future of Canadian youth and to Canada as a whole.
This debate also gave us the opportunity of hearing an excellent speech on the question of education by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and of being informed of the position of the government of our country on this matter.
I also wish to thank the hon. member for Saskatoon for the kind words he had on my behalf because of the speech I made last week in a debate on a similar subject. In his remarks this afternoon, he expressed the wish that I give my opinion on the question he submitted to our consideration. Mr. Speaker, as a man in public life, I have never been afraid to express my opinion, neither here nor elsewhere, and it is with pleasure that I take this opportunity to express my views on the matter he submitted to us.
In the speech he just made, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) told us that the Minister of Justice seemed unaware of the fact that there is a financial crisis in the field of education. I listened most carefully to the remarks of the Minister of Justice and I for one am convinced that he is conscious of the needs felt by all provinces in matters of education. I know that the Minister of Justice is mindful of provincial autonomy and that he leaves to each province the care of discharging its obligations.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Saskatoon when he says that our schools are faced with certain financial difficulties in each and every educational field, primary, secondary and university. Because of the increase in our population we have to build more schools and universities. We also recognize the necessity of providing higher pay for college and university professors as well as for high school and elementary school teachers. These people are putting heart and soul in the teaching of our children and I do think that everybody here will agree that they should be better paid.

Education
Still the problem which we have to face in the educational field also exists in other fields. I need only mention here the difficulties faced by municipalities in their administrative work, precisely because of their current rapid expansion. However, the financial difficulties which we are facing in the educational field are such as to deserve study by all those who are in charge of the various government activities in this country.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, this is a critical problem since it has a bearing on the future of our children, of the younger generation of this country and of the nation as a whole.
In seeking to settle this financial problem, we must take into account the British North America Act in so far as it concerns the rights which have been reserved to the various provinces on confederation.
Last week during a debate initiated by the hon. member for York Centre, I had the opportunity of expressing my views on the attitude that we should adopt here in this house, with regard to education, in order to ensure that provincial autonomy in this connection be respected. In my conclusion I supported the granting of university scholarships which would in no way threaten the autonomy of the provinces, on the contrary.
To return to the discussion now under way, let us read over the resolution submitted by the hon. member for Saskatoon:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of taking steps to relieve the financial crisis in education, without encroaching in any way on the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in this field, by granting financial assistance to the various provinces for the expansion and equalization of educational opportunity across Canada.
When I first read the resolution, I felt inclined to support it. However, after listening to the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for Saskatoon, I think I should make considerable reservations, and perhaps even more than reservations. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to speak of the hon. member personally, but I fear this resolution coming from the C.C.F. benches creates a great danger. Indeed, during the four years I have spent in this house, I have noticed that certain members of his party seemed to forget, on several occasions, that we had in Canada a constitution giving rights to the provinces in certain fields, and more particularly in the field of education. When I read carefully the resolution moved by the hon. member, I see that it included the following sentence:
.	.	. without encroaching in any way on the
exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces . . .
However, while making his speech this afternoon, the hon. member had this to say: "The public of Canada would support, I am quite sure, this plea which I am making for the granting of federal money for education, so long as there was no interference with provincial responsibilities implied".
Earlier, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member had said: "I wonder if it would disturb the constitution too much if the federal government were to assume some of the capital cost of schools". He concludes by saying that he does not believe it would.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the educational system, both on the primary and secondary level, is exclusively within the jurisdiction of the various provincial legislatures. When the hon. member says that we should assume some of the capital cost of schools, we already see there an encroachment upon the autonomy of the provinces, and that is exactly what we do not want.
In that same speech, the hon. member said:
What is taught, how it is taught, and where it is taught or anything else of that kind lies within the jurisdiction of the province. All we want to do is to support the hands of those people within the provinces who are trying to educate these children. That is all we want to do and it is entirely a financial problem.
Well no, Mr. Speaker, it is not solely a financial matter; it is a problem affecting the organization of education in this country and more particularly in the provinces, a prerogative which has been guaranteed to us by the British North America Act which provides that education is exclusively a provincial matter.
In the province of Quebec, as in any other Canadian province, I am sure that the legislative body wishes to discharge its responsibilities in accordance with the rights and powers guaranteed by the constitution. That is what is provided by section 93. As I said last week, when we have to deal with education we must be very careful to respect that guarantee given to the provinces by the fathers of confederation.
It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot accept in its entirety the resolution moved by the hon. member for Saskatoon; I wonder if the hon. member realizes the difference between what we could call here education proper, which comes under provincial jurisdiction, and Canadian culture, a field where the government of our country

may have, in some cases, certain responsibilities. I agree with the hon. member when he says that our educational system is in great need of funds. Since the planning of education has been entrusted to the provinces the solution of this financial problem in the field of secondary and primary education is their sole responsibility. Therefore, as a representative of a federal constituency, I will not even discuss these problems in so far as they relate to primary and secondary education.
In the field of university education, the problem is just as serious. However, who provides the universities with the funds they require to educate our children? These funds come from credits voted by the different provincial legislatures, in certain cases from federal grants, and from certain amounts put at the disposal of our universities by private enterprise or by private individuals anxious to help our young Canadians.
Needs are growing, Mr. Speaker, precisely because more and more young people, throughout this country, are entering university. I am happy to note that fact. It proves that Canadian culture is constantly being raised to higher levels, and this is as it should be. I had occasion last week to express my views on the matter of primary and secondary education. As I said a while ago, it is different in the case of universities. In fact, there is in that field a cultural aspect regarding which the federal government could make a contribution without however laying down any condition. That is in complete agreement with the findings of the Massey report which recommended assistance to universities, which is urgently required.
For a long time the Prime Minister of our country has been concerned with the problems of universities. Recently, when he received an honorary degree from the University of Sherbrooke, he announced that he would recommend to parliament that grants to universities be increased from 50 cents to $1 for each university student in the country, thus bringing to $16 million annually the amount of statutory federal grants to universities.
In the speech he made on November 12 last at the national conference of Canadian universities, the right hon. Prime Minister said, and I am quoting from La Presse of Tuesday November 13, 1956:
I have already explained why the federal government had the right to offer such assistance. I feel that it is not only its right but its duty to do so.
In the same speech the Prime Minister added:
My colleagues and I feel that the annual federal grants to universities should be continued and
Education
increased and we are prepared to recommend to parliament, at the next regular session, that they be doubled.
That is what the parliament of Canada has done at the very beginning of this session. And if I refer to Hansard of last Friday, January the 15th, I see that the Prime Minister in the explanations he gave us on the subject of the assistance that the Canadian government wants to give to various universities in this country, takes into account the autonomy of the provinces. During the same debate I noticed that the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), agreed with the Prime Minister. I suggest that all the members of the house recognize that we should help Canadian universities. However, I want to be sure that such assistance will be granted with due respect for the autonomy of the universities and provinces. In order to insure that this autonomy will not be affected, it is provided in the measure introduced by the government that the universities of the various provinces of the country will not be forced to accept the grants, but that they can refuse them if they believe that this would encroach upon the autonomy of the provinces.
The resolution of the government provides that the grants will be distributed by an independent organization.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) said a moment ago that there was no difference between the measure introduced by the Prime Minister and the proposal of the hon. member for Saskatoon. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickers-gill) pointed out that there is all the difference in the world between these two proposals since under the resolution of the Prime Minister, the grants will be offered to the universities and not directly to the provinces.
Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a special appeal to private enterprise in this country to provide an ever increasing help to our universities and our university students.
I also wish to congratulate the hon. members of this house for the interest they have shown in the problems of education and teaching in our country. In so doing, they prove that they are conscious of their responsibilities; I urge them to continue to work for the future of our country with due respect to the spirit and the letter of our Canadian constitution.
The hon. member for Saskatoon said this afternoon that he was glad to find that an ever increasing number of hon. members show their interest in education. However, I would not want the growing interest to

Education
which he referred to be taken as an excuse to encroach upon certain sections of the Canadian constitution.
However, I cannot give my full support to the resolution before the house, precisely on account of the explanations given by the hon. member. In my opinion, if the resolution were carried in its present form, it would be an encroachment upon the constitution and that cannot be allowed. Such an action would be an interference in a field exclusively reserved to provincial jurisdiction. I am still convinced that no hon. member would wish to encroach upon what we call provincial autonomy.

Mr. Speaker, I have very little time left before ten o'clock but I do think I have time enough to make a few remarks. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), I am convinced, has introduced his motion in a sincere effort to find a solution to the problem of education in general.
I do not have to demonstrate the need for supporting education. That is a generally recognized fact. All of us here to the best of our ability, are searching for a formula according to which our young fellow citizens may be allowed to benefit more from education.
Education is a personal responsibility of parents. That is a privilege which is rightfully theirs. Still, man is not able to develop, to realize his whole potentialities except as a member of society. That being the case, those in authority must exercise their complementary duties. In my province this is first of all the business of the local school board to which I am particularly happy to pay tribute.
Our federal system nevertheless recognizes the exclusive responsibilities of the provincial authorities to legislate in educational matters. I will remind hon. members that the fathers of confederation did not deem it wise to include these in the general powers granted to the provinces under section 92. They chose instead to draw up a separate section to deal with this matter, a fact which indicates the importance they attached to the subject. It was their wish that education be a provincial matter. Even with the best intentions in the world, I do not think that we should do anything which would, in any way, diminish the responsibilities of the province.
The mover of the motion has taken the precaution to include the following reservation:
Without encroaching in any way on the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in this field.
That is undeniable recognition of the fact that the federal government has no jurisdiction in that field, and that should be sufficient to dispose of the resolution. Problems coming within the field of our jurisdiction are numerous and varied; some are very difficult to solve. We should spend our time and energy working for the common good of our constituents in the fields in which we have jurisdiction and which were assigned to us by the provisions of the British North America Act.
Federal legislators are duty bound to be very circumspect and careful in matters of education. The province of Quebec has most imperative and special reasons to be jealous of the field of education. It is the only means available to French-speaking Canadians of keeping the language and traditions inherited from their forefathers. If there is a crisis in the field of education, a fact recognized practically everywhere, let us leave to the provincial authorities the trouble of studying the problem and let us help them to solve it if they so request us. The proposals designed to put an end to the present financial crisis in the field of education referred to in the resolution must come from the provinces. They will I am sure set the required conditions and guarantees.
For all the reasons I just gave-it is already ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker

I must say that I will oppose this resolution of the hon. member for Saskatoon and I move the adjournment of the debate.

On motion of Mr. Gauthier (Lake St. John) the debate was adjourned.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. O. White (Middlesex East) moved:
subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act and regulations made under the act, so as to provide a final receipt for those income tax returns filed for the preceding calendar year for individuals whose income is $10,000 or less.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this problem was discussed a year ago but with respect to the resolution I had on the order paper at that time there was some question as to whether it would be ruled out of order by Your Honour, and so I took advantage of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and made some remarks at that time concerning my opinion as to how the changes in the Income Tax Act might apply. Having revised the resolution appearing on the order paper in the meantime, I welcome this opportunity to present to hon. members some of the arguments which I feel are good and valid reasons for some changes and amendments to the Income Tax Act as they apply to those taxpayers whose incomes are not in the high or extra high brackets.

Income Tax Act
One of the first objects that I have heard has always been, "Well, you are drawing a distinction between those who are in receipt of an income of $10,000 and those who are below that figure". I hasten right here to point out that the government now draws a line between various categories or groups of taxpayers, and those in the higher income tax bracket pay a greater percentage of tax. Therefore, to provide for those taxpayers in the lower income group a final settlement 12 months after the 30th day of April in each tax year would not be so difficult. It would not be difficult also because of the fact that, as I understand it, where fraud is charged the income tax department can take almost any number of years and bring the taxpayer before the courts of the land. Therefore, I cannot see that it would be too difficult to administer.
I, therefore, make no apologies, Mr. Speaker, for bringing this matter to the attention of the house and taking up some of the time of the house to present my views, and I think they are the views of a large number of Canadian citizens.
If we believe in democracy-and I think we all do-we acknowledge it is government by the people and for the people not government by a ruling class. Consequently, I think if a poll were taken the vast nfajority of taxpayers would be in favour of some amendment to the act which would let them know when they were finished with one year's business. At this moment I should also like to mention that I doubt whether there are over 5 per cent of the income tax payers in the bracket which I have mentioned whose income could not be revised either way.
As I said on another occasion, if my income tax return or that of any other hon. member or individual taxpayer was submitted to ten different officials or assessors of the income tax branch those gentlemen would come up with ten different answers or maybe 20 if you went back a second time. Consequently I think the time is long past due when some method should be established by which a definite and correct conclusion could be reached. I do not think this would be difficult because it seems to me that any qualified efficiency firm or accounting firm could set up a system to administer the act more speedily and satisfactorily. While I am mentioning these things I might point out that there are many harassed taxpayers who have worried themselves into a premature grave over the problem of income tax. As I said last year, I hold no brief for those persons who deliberately set out to defraud the income tax branch and consequently the Canadian people of what is their just payment

under the law. I also want to point out that in my opinion the vast majority of Canadians are law abiding citizens regardless of what the income tax people may think about this.
I plan to appeal to the reason of both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue. I doubt if we depart from the British system of justice whereunder the accused is innocent until he is proven guilty in any other legal procedure, but people being prosecuted by the income tax branch are considered guilty until they have proved themselves innocent.
As I mentioned previously, I am not alone in bringing to the attention of the government the problems confronting individual taxpayers because many individuals and groups are expressing concern in this regard. I have on my files hundreds of letters from taxpayers in Ontario who have written to me protesting the present system under which they are never certain just where they stand with the income tax branch. In order to point out how widespread is this concern, there are many county councils which have passed resolutions along this line. I am going to refer to just a few of the counties near my constituency. These include Elgin, Huron and Perth, Lanark, Grey and Halton, Bruce, Lincoln, Oxford and Waterloo, Brant-Haldimand, Middlesex and Lambton. There are some others, but at the moment I do not have their resolutions on file. In addition to that many chambers of commerce have protested the present set-up as well as the federation of agriculture, the farmers' union and various women's institutes. I want to mention particularly two groups of women's institutes in Essex, the Malden Women's Institute and the Women's Institute of Essex County. They have both written to me backing up what I had to say a year ago and expressing the hope that some satisfactory solution can be found for the problem.
There have been many editorials and newspaper comments supporting the stand I took, and I should like to refer the government to a couple of clippings which I have and which I think are most pertinent to the problem. We all realize that the government has grown and now reaches into the private life of practically every individual in Canada. History has a habit of repeating itself. I have here a front page editorial which appeared in the Toronto Saturday Night of September 4, 1954. This was commenting upon what had gone on in Great Britain during and at the close of the war, with particular reference to ministerial responsibility to parliament. They were referring to an incident concerning the taking over of a 700-acre farm in Great Britain and what they

say has a bearing on the understanding which the provinces had when they relinquished their taxation rights at the beginning of the war. The resignation of a particular minister in Great Britain had been called for, and the editorial went on to say:
There was a time when such a resignation would have excited little comment: it would have been expected as the only possible course for a minister who had failed to keep his department in good order. But there was surprised and respectful applause for Sir Thomas Dugdale: he had actually admitted that a minister is responsible for the conduct of the civil servants under his direction. In other words, the principle of responsibility has been so generally ignored that any recognition of it by the members or minions of government comes as a distinct shock.
Canadians have had many opportunities in recent years to study the growing disinclination of both federal and provincial cabinet ministers to accept responsibility for the sins of their departments, and considering the complacency with which this ministerial attitude has been accepted, they are likely to see a good deal more of it. There will be no change until they understand that this sort of thing can only mean government not by elected representatives but by an uncontrolled civil service.
When ministers refuse to share the blame for waste, inefficiency and worse in their departments, they are admitting that the job of government has grown too big for them; they are claiming, in effect, that while they should still be trusted with the direction of the nation's business, they should not be expected to worry about the people they have hired for the day-to-day handling of that business. If we condone this attitude, we must be prepared to accept the inevitable result: the end of our control, as electors, over the way we are to be governed.
I commend to the government a second reading of that editorial in their leisure time because it does indicate the drift that is going on in this country toward a certain amount of bureaucracy. Another clipping along the same line rather intrigued me. It reads:
History Repeats Itself
Twenty centuries ago, and thereafter for four hundred years, the Romans ruled Britain without interfering in the private lives of the people. The Roman government attended to its own affairs and allowed the people to attend to theirs. Indeed, as Douglas Jerrold points out in his book "England: Past, Present and Future" it was from the Roman empire that the western world learned the art and purpose of government and the application of the rule or law to the preservation of the lives of free men living in ordered and mutually dependent societies.
However, as I have mentioned before, we see the various departments of government reaching out and trying to control the private lives of individuals from day to day, and it cannot in the end, in my estimation, lead to anything but disaster. For this reason I am asking the department to consider and review its attitude as it applies to the income tax payer in this country. The present attitude is, I believe, having a somewhat disastrous effect, but, no doubt because of the ever-increasing degree of inflation, that effect is
Income Tax Act
not as apparent as it might be in other circumstances. Nevertheless, it is certainly discouraging production and, in a sense, it is penalizing the very people who form the productive element in our nation. When you take in-as I am doing here-that group of people whose net income is less than $10,000 a year, you are covering the vast majority of the productive enterprises of this country.
Some people are saying "I am not going to work for the government any more; I am just going to make a living out of my land or business. I am not going to hire a lot of help in order to make a few dollars. If I should lose, it would be 'just too bad'; if I win, the government will only take it from me and wonder why I did not make any more". Consequently, every small businessman, every self-employed individual and every working man who engages in parttime work has begun to question the results of his efforts as far as his income tax commitment is concerned. They are wondering: "If we do some overtime or put in some extra work for ourselves, will all we have gained be confiscated?" The net result of this situation is that we are in a sense, rewarding the non-productive and punishing those who are productive in our economy.
That is not the whole story either, Mr. Speaker. There is the fear in the minds of many people that sooner or later they will be "hauled on the carpet" and have their business transactions for years past-possibly over the past 15 or 20 years-made subject to review. We in the western world, have been told about the terror in totalitarian countries where the gestapo comes knocking on the door in the night. That is held up as one of the things to be feared in a totalitarian world. Well, the income tax department does not even wait until night before they knock on the door-they come in at any time, represented, in many cases, by a little man with a lot of authority. Yes, I am "sticking my neck out" a long way, as I mentioned earlier. The department seizes your books and seizes your assets, and you are presumably guilty until you are proven innocent. I know whereof I speak. I do not plan, Mr. Speaker, to bring to your attention four individual cases with which I am very familiar, but I will mention two of these cases involving estates. The people concerned were told that they owed the department a sizeable sum of money, and the heirs and the legal firms representing them were afraid to fight the case. Accordingly, they paid. It almost reached a point where it amounted to blackmail rather than the administration of the law.

Income Tax Act
In a couple of other cases in which the people appealed, when they said they were going to take the matter to the income tax appeal board, some time later one of the officials appeared and said, "We have reviewed this whole case; there are some mistakes; we are sorry but there is an error; forget all about it." If those people had paid the amount demanded, it would have been an admission that they were wrong. I am willing to bet that there are many cases in which the people, rather than fight, pay the amount demanded but do not owe the department at all.
Many of these taxpayers-good, law-abiding citizens-are finding that the department are autocratic and overbearing in their approach to the taxpayer. In fact, a good friend of mine retired years ago and went to Devon, England. In England during the war all kinds of restrictions were placed on individuals, as was done here, as we know, through the wartime prices and trade board. I well remember a letter he wrote to me and in which he said, "The government of Britain are making a crook out of every honest Englishman." I venture to say that the income tax department here, through their methods, are making crooks out of many otherwise honest people. I do not know whether I should use the word "warn", but at any rate I think I should tell the department that there is a rising tide of resentment against the department and the methods that are used in collecting what they allege are amounts owing.
I mentioned the small businessman. I want to point out that agriculture is not the only industry affected. Practically all small business across the country is affected. Those large corporations and companies doing a big business have their accounting systems set up; they have men who watch every angle of taxation so as to save as much as they possibly can in every financial move they make. But the smaller income tax payer is not able to hire that expert advice and opinion and consequently he must take his chances. Labour are watching closely so that in the overtime work they do, and by means of which they may contribute to the economy of the country, they are not penalized. They watch their overtime and pay close attention to it. In many cases lawyers advise their clients to settle rather than to fight the department because they figure that if they go to court and fight the matter or antagonize the department, the department will just clamp down on the law firm as well. Consequently they hesitate to take on these accounts.

I know of one particular case in which a certain individual was taking care of accounts for several clients. As soon as that individual died the accounts of every client of his immediately came under surveillance, and they had not anyone to fight their battle. They had expected that this particular individual knew all about their business and could fight the case for them. As soon as he had passed on, there was no one left to fight the battle. Consequently many of them were taken for either large or small sums. I think this is a terrible state of affairs.
Then there are many people who go to the income tax department for advice. But according to what has happened in the courts and in the appeal boards, that is not the place to go for advice.
I hold in my hand a couple of clippings from newspapers, and the heading on one item is, "You take Official Tax Advice at Own Peril". This clipping is from the Ottawa Journal of February 21, 1955 and says that the oral or written statements and opinions of assessors and others when dealing with taxpayers from time to time, however sincerely expressed, can hardly be said to fulfil these requirements of section 14 of the Income Tax Act.
Then I should like to cite what happened to one taxpayer, as illustrated by an article in the London Free Press of March 12, 1956. Evidently this taxpayer in company with his auditor consulted the local officials, his only contact with the department, and they agreed that the cash basis method of computing his income for tax purposes was acceptable to them. However, some years later he was assessed for a considerable sum. He appealed to the income tax appeal board, which board ruled that the taxpayer was overly optimistic in his assumption that the cash method of computing income had been accepted. The joker is the word "accepted" in the act. According to the board the term "accepted" indicates the unqualified acceptance in appropriate form on behalf of the crown which leaves no scope for doubt. The oral or written statements or opinions of assessors or others, however sincerely expressed, cannot be considered as fulfilling this requirement. Consequently, therefore, you must take their advice with a grain of salt because later the department will repudiate it. I feel this is a regrettable state of affairs because these small taxpayers about whom I am talking should be able to obtain correct advice from the department. However, experience has proven that advice is not dependable.
A little earlier I mentioned the chamber of commerce brief. The chamber of commerce recommended that the right to assess

be limited to a one-year period dating from the assessment. There is a joker in that, too, Mr. Speaker, and I claim that is not good enough. Some assessments are delayed for years and the taxpayer does not know his position. It provides a loophole and an alibi for the department. The Department of National Revenue demands that the individual taxpayer's returns be in four months after the close of the calendar year. However, when it comes to the department processing these returns, that can go on for years and years without arriving at any finality.
Just last evening on the train coming to Ottawa I met some of the members of the legislative and without asking them for their opinions on the subject they expressed concern about the lack of finality and suggested that something should and could be done about it. While I am mentioning that I might say that I think there is a desire on the part of the taxpayer to have a clear definition of capital gains. There is no such clear definition today. I would say that if the government is as efficient as they would lead the public to believe there is no reason in the world why these returns could not be processed within 12 months from April 30.
There is another alarming angle. I suppose there are two sides to every story, but I have had several taxpayers come to me and say that the assessors who appeared at their places demanded cash and would not take a cheque. I suppose there is a possibility of someone giving a cheque that would bounce, and consequently they did not want to be caught that way. On the other hand, I am just wondering why they demanded cash. In my opinion that angle should be investigated because the demand does not ring true.

subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext: Would my hon. friend give particulars on that?

subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
No, sir, I am not going to divulge the names of the people who came to me. They are in sufficient trouble now. Last year, Mr. Speaker, there were quite a number of Liberal members who had resolutions on the order paper or mentioned in their speeches the problems I am bringing to the attention of the house today. I would hope these members would be influential in furthering the cause about which I am speaking this afternoon. I noticed that there was one member on the government side who had the courage of his convictions and made a speech accordingly.
There are those who will say this cannot be done. I would think such an answer by the government or the officials concerned would be an admission of inefficiency
Income Tax Act
or an admission that the department does not want to settle individual accounts within any stated time. It would be an admission also that the officials of the department like the power with which they are vested and are loath to relinquish it.
Recently I had two cases brought to my attention. One man had been making returns for many years when he was approached and told that his account was incorrect. He was asked for quite a sum of money and said he did not have that kind of money, but he would allot a certain percentage of his monthly pay cheque to meet their account. This was agreed upon. The account was reduced from thousands to hundreds. Then his wife was taken sick and she was in and out of hospital for many months. When the due date for the next income tax payment rolled around the man informed the department he could not pay it because he did not have the cash. He was informed that his wages would be garnisheed. He pointed out to the department that the refundable portion of the amount deducted from his wages for income tax purposes would more than cover what he owed the department, but they would not agree to that. They garnisheed his wages. As hon. members know, in the case of some companies this means that you are let out of your job.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext: Will my hon. friend give me the particulars of that?

subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
Yes, sir. I had a letter from an individual who said that apparently her only crime was saving money for her old age. When the income tax department found cash in the bank they were immediately suspicious and investigated every possible angle. Her conclusion was that all the government wanted to do was to worry her to death before she was 70 and able to collect the old age pension.
A year ago I mentioned the efficiency of Eaton's and Simpson's in keeping track of their customers' accounts.
The Minister of Finance rather questioned what I had to say. I therefore took the trouble to find out how many accounts Eaton's and Simpson's processed in their mail order departments in a day and how many employees they had. As I understand it, the Eaton company employs about 5,000 people in its mail order department. This has nothing to do with the retail sales. They service about 50,000 orders a day and the average time taken to process an order is 20 minutes. The income tax department employ over 6,000 people. There are approximately 9 million people of tax-paying age in the country. They are not all taxpayers. I did not have time to review the

Income Tax Act
income tax statistics to find out exactly the number, but there are in Canada about 1,500 persons for each employee in the income tax department, to say nothing of those who are not eligible for taxation. Therefore, it would seem to me that there could be a great deal more efficiency employed by the department than is employed at the present time.
While what I have to say now has nothing to do with the settling of accounts yearly, I do want to point out that those persons who are contributing to approved pension plans are able to deduct from their income tax the amount paid for such a plan, but those who are individually or self-employed help to pay for it because industry or concern passes on those costs. They become part of the cost of doing business. Consequently, those people who are individually or self employed are not able to deduct any payments they might make to a pension plan of their own. They are, in a sense, contributing to the pension plans of others in the costs of things they have to buy. That is something the department should look into. All self-employed people are under that kind of double-edged sword arrangement. On the one hand they are paying for others and on the other they are not able to deduct the costs of their own plans.
There is another comment I wish to make. We saw this during the early part of the last session. Planes and many other pieces of war goods were declared surplus and obsolete. They were bought as junk at a fraction of their original cost. Then, after being purchased as junk, they were sold to belligerent countries in the Middle East. My contention is that if some of the money obtained was used for hospitalization plans, increases in pensions and things like that for our own Canadian people it would be putting money to much better use.
I also wish to point out that it would take a Philadelphia lawyer to understand the Income Tax Act. The department expects individuals who are busy trying to run their own business to understand all the ramifications of the act.
In conclusion I wish to point out, Shakespeare said that life is a stage and every person plays a part. I think everyone knows the part the income tax department is playing, with eminent success.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this subject is not new to the house. As a matter of fact, last session we had a very worth-while debate on a subject very close to the resolution we are discussing now because of the introduction of an amendment

to a statute by the hon. member for Kamloops. At that time the hon. member for Middlesex East, who is now proposing this resolution, spoke and he said, as reported at page 3237 of Hansard:
The income tax is probably the fairest method of collecting taxes because those who are most able to pay are the ones from whom taxes are taken. But the way in which it is done at the present time is extremely unsatisfactory.
I take it that in essence this is still the reason for his bringing forward this resolution today. On the other hand, I want to remind him and the house that last year when this matter was under discussion it was indicated that while the government at that time had under its income tax provisions an opportunity to reassess, beyond conditions of fraud and misrepresentation, a taxpayer's return within a period of six years, consideration would be given to reducing that opportunity in regard to time. In August of last year, when the Income Tax Act was amended by this house, it was proposed as a government measure that this period of time within which re-assessment could take place under normal conditions be reduced from six years to four years. It is true that the public bill, as introduced by the hon. member for Kamloops, proposed three years, but I suggest to the house it is reasonable to think that this fairly important reduction passed last year, from six years to four years, is worthy of a try-out without the most radical suggestion made by the hon. member for Middlesex East.
Some complications would result if we were to accept at its face value the proposition of the hon. member for Middlesex East. While there is some vagueness in the wording, he suggests that we can within a year of filing arrive at a conclusion with respect to the tax obligation of all individuals filing tax claims.
Our laws also provide a certain number of privileges to the taxpayers. It is not clear in the hon. member's resolution that he would similarly want to restrict the taxpayer in so far as his rights are concerned in asking for re-assessment in the case of a deduction at source. Under the present law the taxpayer is given the privilege of two years within which to ask the taxation department to refund to him certain moneys that he considers due by reason of certain deductions that are provided under law. That is not clear and if we were to accept the hon. member's resolution as proposed this afternoon I suggest it would take away from the taxpayer whose income is taxed at the source privileges that he now has of two years' opportunity of applying to

the income tax department for a re-assessment and a reconsideration of his tax payments and his application for a refund for lawful deductions.
In the legislation proposed by the hon. member for Kamloops last year there was at least recognition of the fact that there should not be restrictions for the department in so far as taxpayers are concerned in cases of fraud and misrepresentation. In the resolution that has been presented to us this afternoon I find no reservation with respect to that matter and I think it will commend itself to the house as unworthy of acceptance on that score alone, because surely the present opportunities of the income tax department should be furthered and continued in terms of being able to reassess in the case of taxpayers regarding whom there is very definite evidence of fraud and misrepresentation in the matter of their filing.
