The hon. member covered
that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
It is not in the resolution. If we were to accept the resolution I know my hon. friend who just rose would be among the first to say we passed a resolution which was not accepted holus-bolus as a government.
Another thing which I think should be taken into consideration by hon. members is the general element of justice and fairness in tax matters as it relates to all taxpayers across the country. I find that in the most recent publication of the Department of National Revenue entitled "Taxation Statistics for 1956" and which is based on tax returns for the year 1954 the following information is available to all of us. It is reported there that the total number of taxable income returns for the year 1954 was 3,410,160. The number of non-taxable returns was 1,393,250. This means that a grand total of 4,803,410 tax returns were considered by the officials of the Department of National Revenue in 1954. I submit to the common sense of hon. members that they would not want to employ in the Department of National Revenue on a peak work period basis and then a lay-off basis the number of employees who would be required from April 30 to the end of the calendar year to process that number of returns.
I know the proposer of this proposition is sincere in his suggestion and I also know that generally speaking he speaks for an agricultural community. I want to point out to him that the taxation statistics for the year 1954 to which I have referred show that out of a total of 4,800,000 returns only 43,000 farmers and fishermen submitted returns that were subsequently found to be
Income Tax Act
taxable. In addition there were 171,000 farmers and fishermen who submitted returns that were non-taxable.
There are many hon. members of this house who represent ridings which are basically composed of wage earners who have income from only one source and that is from an employer. Respecting the employees' class, a total of 3,032,300 employees filed returns on income that was taxable and a total of 994,660 employees filed returns on income that was not taxable. If we are to regard the element of fairness, I do not think the mass of people whose basic income is taxed at the source for income tax purposes as a result of their being employees would be satisfied if they felt that this government or any other government was restricted, as is suggested by the resolution before us, in its opportunity to examine carefully the returns of other taxpayers who have a more complicated situation, such as business proprietors, farmers and fishermen and professionals, in order to assure that everybody is paying the just and proper rates that are passed by this parliament.

subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has so aptly put it, it is not so much the collection of taxes or the rates charged that is objected to, but rather it is the method of collecting taxes that is objected to, and that is what is behind the resolution of the hon. member for Middlesex East.
I suppose, Mr. Speaker, tax collectors and tax collecting methods have been unpopular throughout history. As many hon. members probably know, in the old and difficult days of the Romans the job of tax collector was hired out at a certain price. In other words, if the government of the day wanted a certain amount of taxes collected from a given area and they expected, let us say, the equivalent of $100,000 to come from a specific part of the country, someone would contract to take the job and if they succeeded in collecting more than $100,000 in taxes they filled their own pockets with the surplus. We all know, of course, that such a thing would not be allowable today; however, in effect it may not be as unallowable as it might appear because while the tax collectors of today receive a salary I think some of them have the attitude which says, "Get all you can". I know of one particular instance which comes to mind and there are other instances which I could cite. Just recently in my own town a man who operates a small business was visited by the collectors who said, "Well, we got so much out of so and so and now we are

Income Tax Act
going to see how much we can get out of you". If that is the attitude of the tax collectors it is little wonder that the general public is complaining about the methods used by the officials of the Department of National Revenue because the state of mind represented by the "get all you can" attitude is not a desirable one.
There are people in other positions who have the same type of attitude. For instance, it is often believed that some policemen like to get as many convictions as possible because they think they might earn a promotion on this account. I cannot help but feel that a great many junior officials of the Department of National Revenue have the feeling that the more they can get out of the people the greater will be their chances of promotion. I know full well that when this department was before the special committee on estimates last year the minister denied that this was the case. I am not suggesting that the minister was trying to mislead anyone, as I think he sincerely believes what he said. I do not suppose for a minute that the department condones such a state of affairs, but I am quite sure in my own mind that many of the junior officials feel that if they do a good job and bring in a lot more revenue they are going to get promoted. I cannot help feeling that that is so as it is only human nature to feel that if you are making a success of your job you are going to get a promotion.
Another thing that was brought' out last year when the affairs of the Department of National Revenue were being considered by the special committee was the length of time books of a company or an individual would be retained by the departmental officials when they were on a fishing expedition. Several times I have mentioned in the house the case of a private company where the books were taken by the departmental officials for examination. The officials arrived at the home of the owner at six o'clock in the morning. The owner was in Europe with his wife, but his son was there. The officials ransacked the house for the books, and I suppose in doing so they were within the law as they had a warrant. These books were kept for over a year, I believe for 15 months, at great inconvenience to the company. For instance, they did not know what money was owing to them because their accounts receivable book was away. They did not know what money they owed because their accounts payable ledger was away.
I see no reason why the department should keep books for that length of time. There is no reason why they could not have books of this kind photostatted and use the photostats

in making their investigation. On previous occasion reference has been made to how good the Department of National Revenue is at photostatting. There is no reason why they could not use methods of that kind in this type of case so that the books might be returned and permit businesses of this type to carry on.
The hon. member who has just resumed his seat has said that he feels one year might be too short a time, that we should try out the four-year period, as was agreed to last year. There may be something in what he says, but I cannot help but feel that if the period was reduced to one year it would work out very well. I know the department will say that this would place a terrific strain on the department, that it would be an incredible thing to do, but I think most hon. members have seen examples in other fields where people have had to do something and have gone out and done it. Many of us can remember when during the war the length of military training was reduced. The usual length of training was from six months to a year but during the war we had to have people in a hurry. In my own experience in the navy the length of training was from three to four months. The results may not have been perfect but I know the people in that branch of the service did a pretty good job even though they had to get their training in a hurry. The same sort of argument could be applied to the Department of National Revenue. When people know they have only a certain length of time to do things they will get them done.
There is another item I should like to mention, the drawing up of income tax returns. As everyone knows, this is an exceedingly complicated matter. I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) agreed that this is so. In fact it is so much so that sometimes people go to lawyers to have this done. I do not think many lawyers know much about this sort of thing. I know I do not and I have an accountant draw up mine for me. A great many other people do the same thing.
However, many people, such as farmers, do not know just whom to go to in order to have their income tax returns drawn up. They should go to a chartered or public accountant, but very often they do not. As I say, many lawyers do not know too much about it but they still go ahead and draw up these forms, but they are responsible for any mistakes they may make on behalf of their clients. On the other hand, many people will go to a township clerk to have their income tax returns drawn up. They do this in perfectly good

faith but, as hon. members know, this presents a very complicated problem in completing the returns, allowing for depreciation and so on.
Someone may go to a township clerk and the township clerk makes a mistake. Then several years later the farmer may find that he owes a lot of money plus interest. He may not be penalized because there was no intent to defraud, but he does have to pay interest. Yet he had his income tax return made out in completely good faith by someone who held himself out as knowing what he was doing. The township clerk holds himself out as an agent who knows and the farmer is penalized. It seems to me that if someone holds himself out as an agent to know, as we call it in law, and draws up income tax returns, he should be liable in damages for any mistakes he may make. If a lawyer makes a mistake he is liable for the consequences. I think that should apply to these other people.
The hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) who proposed this resolution said that there are many practical reasons why the burden of proof should be shifted. The individual must now prove that he is not guilty. I cannot help but feel that this constitutes a dangerous precedent. It may be all very well for government officials to go on fishing expeditions to see what they can find out, for a year as proposed in the resolution, but it is a dangerous precedent. This is contrary to all the principles of British justice which apply throughout the Englishspeaking world, and it is a very dangerous thing. Once it gets into one department of government the next thing we know it will be the case with all departments.
As has been mentioned by the hon. member for Middlesex East, quite often a person will be assessed a certain amount of tax but rather than appeal it to the income tax appeal board, which might entail employing a lawyer, he may decide to pay even though he feels he is not liable. Lawyers may not charge as much as members of some other professions, but they do charge fairly well. You may require a specialist in income tax law which is going to cost more. Even though a man wins his appeal where the sum involved is fairly small he may not be any further ahead.
Quite often a man decides to pay the amount he is assessed for because he feels that even if he won his case it would not be worth it. There might be $500 involved, and even though he wins he might have to pay half that amount to his lawyer. This is the rather unfortunate state of affairs that exists.
Income Tax Act
I appreciate that that is not strictly the fault of the government, but that is what results from this type of law.
There is one last thing I would like to mention. After a reassessment is made a man may find that he owes $4,000 or $5,000. If he is a small businessman or a farmer and has to get that amount of money right away he may find himself in difficulty. I know that at times the Department of National Revenue will allow a little time for payment, but they do not have to. If a small businessman or farmer has to raise $4,000 or $5,000 or $6,000 in a hurry it may well mean the ruination of his business or his farm. We all know that when you have to sell something in a hurry you cannot realize its full value. If a farmer has to sell part of his farm or if a businessman has to sell some of his stock-in-trade in a hurry he may find that he must sell at a considerable discount and thus suffer a heavy loss in relation to what he has to pay. I would like to point out that though the words "fraud and misrepresentation" were not contained in the resolution, the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) dealt with that aspect, and said that this was in no way intended as a means of covering up people who had been dishonest and who had tried to cheat the government of its just due.
The last point I would try to make is this: when it is found that people have not paid what they should have paid, then, though perfectly innocent of any intention to deceive, they are not only penalized by having to pay the amount claimed plus interest, but they often have to suffer a considerable loss in being forced to sell part of a farm or business in order to raise funds in a hurry. I think that if he does nothing else, the Minister of Finance might consider some amendment to the act under which a time limit would be allowed so that people would not have to ruin themselves in an effort to raise money regardless of the circumstances.

speechtext:
I cannot help but feel that more than once in cases where this house has had government resolutions, even government bills, before it for consideration, all has not been stated; in fact, very few government resolutions give a clear picture of the full import of what is intended. Indeed, it often happens that this house, having passed a bill in the belief that it knew what it was doing, finds later that regulations have been attached to that bill to give it an effect which was never intended by the house itself when it passed the measure.
The parliamentary assistant referred to the fact that the taxpayer is given two years in which to claim reassessment and refund. It does occur to me that there might be a strong argument there for saying that the government, or the Department of National Revenue, should also be limited to two years with regard to its own actions; what is fair for the taxpayer on one hand should also be perfectly fair for the department. There is a difference between the two. The department has the wherewithal to hire experts to complete their job, while the individual is often an overworked, oppressed person who has all too little time and, possibly, all too little ability when it comes to keeping books.
I think it is inevitable that the national revenue department should be the most unpopular department of government. After all, they are in the business of collecting taxes, and none of us likes taxes. I think, myself, that the department becomes unpopular in relation to the weight with which taxation bears down on the public. During times like the present when most people believe that taxes are particularly oppressive there is bound to be considerably more criticism. I do feel, however, that the Department of National Revenue and the government can rid themselves of a good deal of the criticism which presently falls upon them by making a concerted effort to remove the anomalies and the inconsistencies which are found within the act itself.
I noticed in the press this morning that only within the last few days the Canadian Bar Association, I believe, and the accountants have made representations to the Department of Finance urging the removal from the act of certain obvious anomalies. I shall not refer to these anomalies in detail, though I could; they are there, and certainly consideration should be given to the correction of this difficulty.

It is also true, Mr. Speaker, that right across the country we find a great variation in the interpretation of the regulations; one finds a difference between the interpretation made by two district offices, in some instances, within a single province. I happen to have had evidence of a certain case which was handled by one of the district offices. It was discovered that the taxpayer in question was the responsibility of another district, and the accounts were accordingly transferred. However, in the second district a different interpretation was placed upon various sections of the act. I sometimes wonder, in this connection, how much of the time of the head office staff here in Ottawa is occupied in correcting errors made in district offices-errors of actual calculation and errors in interpretation. I doubt very much if we will get that information, but from what I hear via the "grapevine" a very substantial part of the time of head office is occupied in straightening out the difficulties which are constantly and chronically arising in the district offices.
That leads me to suggest this: I wonder if the department is doing enough to familiarize its employees in district offices with interpretations as accepted by head office. What effort is made to bring the staff together to consider and study interpretations? I think, myself, that no matter what is being done in this connection more should be undertaken. I agree with the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that it is probably these administrative difficulties that are causing the greatest amount of trouble.
Consider, for example, a farmer who has not either the time or, possibly, the ability- I am only thinking of certain cases; I am not condemning all farmers, or anyone else for that matter-to keep a clear record of his accounts. It does happen that in many cases people have neither the time nor the ability to organize an acceptable accounting system. In these cases the department imposes upon such people what it calls a "net worth statement". In some respects these things are perfectly vicious. I have known the affairs of certain individuals and I have examined net worth statements and, believe me, though you know they are wrong you just cannot prove they are wrong. It is one of the strangest things I have encountered while in public office.
Then there is the practice of placing the onus upon the taxpayer himself; in other words, the department will sometimes set down an almost fantastic figure and say: "We say this is right. If it is not, you prove it is wrong."
I will give the house a typical example- something that recently happened. A farmer

had among his papers a receipt for $1,200, money that he had spent to buy cattle. The department had it included as income and kept insisting that he account for this $1,200. It is almost unbelievable. I would not have believed it myself if I had not seen these papers and the receipt. This is the sort of thing that causes annoyance and aggravation. I sometimes think that when the Department of National Revenue recruits new personnel it does not give sufficient attention to-if I may use this word-training its men.
After all, there are right ways and there are wrong ways of dealing with the public. I should think that the Department of National Revenue would be more concerned than any other department in dealing with them in the right way. They can be firm. They can insist upon the provisions of the act being adhered to. But I am sometimes troubled by the attitudes of those who can-I think someone in a previous debate described them as little gods-and do create a certain animosity among taxpayers or prospective taxpayers. The situation is just not good. I sometimes think that these regulations we now have seem to be predicated upon a premise or assumption held by some that people are inherently dishonest. People are not inherently dishonest. I think it is an error on the part of the Department of National Revenue to create the impression that that is what they sometimes believe. Rather, I would say that it would be an admission that the administration is incompetent, and that in so many cases they try to cover up their incompetence by these unfair procedures and pressures which are imposed upon prospective taxpayers.
I want to say to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance that I think we have come a long way in the past few years in clarifying income tax returns. I think it has been a progressive step. The department are simplifying them to a considerable degree and on the income tax forms they are putting a good deal of information for the purpose of assisting the one who is filing or preparing the return to complete the return with less chance of error. I wish to commend the department for that improvement.
As does the hon. member for Oxford, I feel there is still room for considerable improvement in the field of administration. I will frankly state to you, Mr. Speaker, that I am not fully aware of all the implications in reducing this to a one-year period. However, I would say this. If two years is considered good for the taxpayer on the one hand, certainly it should be considered good enough for the Department of National Revenue on the other hand.
There is just one other thing I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, and it is in connection with 82715-45
Income Tax Act
some of the things that annoy people. A perfectly honest person, we will say, files a return. He completes it to the very best of his ability. Some time later he is informed that he owes more money and of course he is frequently called upon to pay interest on what he owes the department. Yet the department itself can hold a taxpayer's money for quite a considerable period of time but he has no right to claim anything whatsoever by way of interest. It appears that the only safe thing for the average taxpayer to do is to overpay. Then, of course, he is caught again because, Mr. Speaker, in overpaying he runs into financial difficulties, is obliged to borrow and is up against possibly an even higher interest rate. I have said before and I say again that if the department expects me to pay interest on what I owe them, surely the least I can expect is for them to pay me some interest not on what they owe me but on the amount of money which they took from me over and above what the law of the land requires me to pay.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few brief remarks on this matter. First of all, I want to refer to what was said by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. He pointed out one or two technical omissions in the resolution, notably one referring to fraud, and I think that was answered. I think what we are all trying to do is to reach a reasonable solution of this matter. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I would hope that before this debate concluded we would have a somewhat detailed statement not merely from the finance department who look at the principles of taxation matters and decide them, but also from the revenue department who have the business of actually doing the work of collecting. It seems to me that this is rather a question of what is reasonable from a technical point of view rather than in any sense a matter of principle. We are none of us talking about matters of principle, except the principle of being fair. In order to know what is fair one must have a picture of the technique involved in the actual business of collecting.
In the discussion of a year ago, on June 12, 1956, the Minister of National Revenue gave us some figures indicating the way in which the work of the Department of National Revenue had been catching up with arrears of previous years. As reported at page 4959 of Hansard of 1956 he said this:
I am very happy to say that that backlog of work has been cleaned up and we are now on a current basis. The same amount of work, or considerably more work, is now being done with 6,000 to 7,000 employees that was formerly done by 11,000 or more.

Income Tax Act
I come back to what I said a moment ago. What we are all trying to do is to find out what is reasonable or what can be reasonably expected of the department. It is for that reason that I wish we could have a more technical statement giving us a picture of the actual delays that are involved. I would hope that this resolution would not merely be voted down but that it would be taken by the government as a basis for further consideration and that there would be full explanation. If the actual proposal contained in this resolution cannot be fully accepted, then perhaps it can be partly accepted. The people who ought to be able to tell us about the matter are those who are in the day-to-day business of administering the taxes.
I do not think that I need to spend further time in speaking on the matter. I have not before me definite illustrations of the hardship which is being caused, although I think we need have no doubt that hardship is being caused.
I was particularly impressed by a remark made in the course of the debate a year ago-and I think it has been repeated again this afternoon-about the difficulty which is caused to people who find it almost impossible to keep their records in apple-pie order over the years and who, when faced with something that happened years ago, are in great embarrassment. I suppose it is also true to say that even though the amounts involved may not be large, nevertheless many people, notably farmers, have a much more difficult task in making up their income tax returns than do many of those who live in the city, particularly those who are on a salary basis or a semi-salary basis. Their problem is a piece of cake compared with the problem of the farmer. It therefore seems to me that every effort should be made to shorten the time and that the department should show itself to be co-operative in so doing.

Yes, it was. I notice that the parliamentary assistant said that it was reasonable that this system be tried out for a few years. But in answer to that proposal, I suggest it is just as reasonable or more reasonable to ask the department, who are experts in this matter, to consider carefully whether they cannot come up and say, "Yes, we can do it in less than four years. We have reviewed the situation and we are able , to say that we can do it in less than four years."
That leaves one point that I want to make. It may be that certain reservations must be

made. I think we have all agreed that fraud must be expected. In the case of fraud we realize that no arrangement can stand merely because it has existed over a certain number of years. Now, there may be some other qualifications. There may be a qualification which I am not able to put into apt words where new facts arise and where perhaps the matter should be opened up. I realize that is difficult to do, and I realize that may open the door very wide. Perhaps to some extent I am unintentionally torpedoing my friend's resolution when I say that, but my point is merely this. I think we might ask the department not to take an arbitrary position and say that a year ago we reduced it to four years, and we are not going to consider it any further for some years to come. My request of the department is that they take a fair look at the subject. A suggestion has been made that they should have two years just as an individual has two years.
If an argument in detail is made by the department showing that is not fair then the mover of the resolution and other people who have supported it, who are fair minded men, I am sure would be convinced. I do suggest it is fair that they should have a chance to be convinced, and when I say "a chance to be convinced", I mean there should be a reasoned and detailed argument made as to what really is the time required.

The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has just said he had no definite illustration of unfairness. I should like to bring to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, a case decided by the income tax appeal board on October 29, 1956. The judgment was handed down by Mr. Fordham. The case concerned an elderly gentleman in western Ontario who had farmed all his life and who had always been fond of horses. Eventually, he acquired a horse which managed to win for several years. Later on the assessors made an examination of his books and ascertained, by the net worth method, that he had more money than they would have expected from a perusal of his income tax returns. As a consequence, they

assessed him and the assessment took place over a number of years from 1947 onward.
This gentleman filed a notice of appeal, and after the notice was filed the total assessment was reduced by some $7,093. In other words, the department admitted that the original assessment was not correct. I should like to quote from some of the facts cited in Mr. Fordam's judgment.
It may be observed at this point that in the returns for the years 1947 to 1951, inclusive, appellant mentioned having received in the United States of America "race horse purses only". No amounts were mentioned, but in the part of each return in which this acknowledgment was made there is no space provided for the showing of any amounts, in any event.
Then, later in the judgment there is this observation:
As already observed, the appellant obediently reported in the appropriate place in each of his income tax returns for the years 1947, 1948, 1949, 1950 and 1951 that he had received race-horse purses in the United States of America, but this disclosure has availed him nothing. He might well have been asked for particulars of these purses as and when the returns were received and examined. Likely, he would then have learned, before it was too late, that the incidence of income tax rendered desirable the keeping of a careful record of all prize money received across the border. I find it rather difficult to comprehend why no attention was paid to appellant's clear reference to moneys earned by him in the neighbouring country. It is easy to see how he may have been lulled into a feeling of security in the matter when no questions were put to him by local assessors.
It has been considered for some years that race horse winnings would be capital gains. This man had reported to the department the receipt of the money and the department had done nothing about it. Then eight years later they come to him and he is assessed a great amount of money. Let us not forget this assessment was arrived at by the net worth method, and Mr. Ford-ham had a word to say about that:
There is something unsatisfactory about arbitrary assessments as they are necessarily founded on estimate and conjecture to a large extent and these methods of approach leave ample room for error on the part of the computer.
Of course the computer in this case is the department. I am bringing this case to the attention of the house because although the taxpayer has reported the source of the income he was not asked to explain it nor was he told that the amount would be taxable. As Mr. Fordham points out, it certainly does not seem fair at this stage. I feel it is manifestly unfair to assess a man who is 69 years of age some eight years after he has reported income and upon which he has not been questioned in any manner whatever.
There are other instances of gross unfairness in the establishing of taxable income on the net worth basis. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, we come down to the fact that 82715-45J
Income Tax Act
the administration of the department does not dispense British justice. According to the department the taxpayer is guilty until proven innocent, but I believe that he should be innocent until proven guilty.

I am assuming, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) will be replying to some of the comments that have been made about this motion. My object in rising, chiefly, is to ask a number of questions for the purpose of clarification. Perhaps the hon. member would be kind enough to make a note of the questions because I would appreciate an explanation.
First, I want to say that if the principle of the resolution is to bring about, at some point, finality to the income tax cases of individuals then I feel that the principle is a good one. It is a cause of irritation and disturbing for people to have their income tax affairs gone over year after year without reaching a point at which they can say, I have fulfilled my obligations to the government; the case is closed. It would appear to me that the intention behind the motion is good and on that basis the motion has merit.
One thing that bothers me is, I was going to say the haziness of the motion, but I do not wish to be too hard on the mover. It appears to me there are a number of questions left unanswered. Just looking at the second last line of the motion, I find these words:
. . . a final receipt for those whose income tax returns filed for the preceding calendar year . . .
The question that arises in my mind is this. Is that a final receipt, as is stated in the motion, for the income tax return? .
If it means exactly what it says, then I am a little doubtful as to whether it really is the intention because I would imagine the hon. member means a final receipt for income tax obligations or assessments rather than the returns themselves.
Then, it goes on to say, "for the preceding calendar year". I am thinking of something of this nature. Suppose I, as an individual taxpayer, were slow in filing my income tax returns, as unfortunately many of us are at times, and suppose I filed for the calendar year 1956 in November 1957, which I do not suggest is a good example but it could happen, then, what is the purport of the resolution? Is it that I should receive a final receipt for the preceding calendar year? Surely, one would not expect to receive a final receipt for the preceding calendar year if he filed within a month or two of the next calendar year. That would be, of course, an impossible and unreasonable thing

Income Tax Act
to expect. Then, if he did not receive it that year and it carried over into the next year then, of course, he would not be receiving a receipt for the preceding calendar year. This is one of the things I would like to have explained.
Then, the resolution states further, "for individuals whose income is $10,000 or less". I would like the hon. member to tell us what he means by "income of $10,000 or less". Does he mean gross income, net income or taxable income? If he means taxable income, then, of course, we understand his point, but again I would like him to explain, if he will be so good as to do so.

Another question which arises is, what happens in connection with refunds? Again, I wish to say that if the intention or the principle of the motion is that as quickly as possible after the returns have been filed the case should be brought to a point of finality, then I feel the motion has merit, but as it stands now there are some grave doubts in my mind as to what is exactly meant by the motion itself and I hope the hon. member will be kind enough to give us an explanation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there can be no question that, in accordance with the established principles of British justice, a sword should not be permitted to hang over the heads of our people. That is exactly the situation with regard to the very long period of time during which an assessment can be made against any citizen in Canada in regard to his income tax.
I have had some experience in police work over the years and I have some knowledge of the methods by which investigations are carried out. The criterion of success of any investigator in the income tax branch is usually the amount of money he can bring in or the assessments he can increase.

demand that the citizens of a free land be given greater consideration than they are given at the present time in regard to income tax assessments.

Having said that, I would point out I am perfectly conscious of the fact that wage earners do not have much leeway inasmuch as their income tax is deducted at source and their position is different from that of the small businessman who sometimes is not able to hire the most qualified bookkeepers and accountants and therefore has to deal with a problem of considerable importance; but I am thinking more particularly of the farmer who is confronted with the problem of having to make out an income tax return that completely meets the requirements of the act and the regulations thereunder without perhaps there being any leeway to question certain items. Concerning the matter of keeping records and books, I think some progress has been made and even the problem of the farmer is being worked out in a more satisfactory manner than was the case a while ago, but nonetheless the farmer is in a peculiar situation which is admittedly difficult. I return to the matter of the desirability of having the income tax people demonstrate in some manner to the public that they are friends of the taxpayer rather than being viewed with fear or as something to be avoided.
The final comment I wish to make relates to cases where there is a suspicion of wrongdoing or fraud and steps are taken to carry out an investigation. Unfortunately I have heard of cases where the investigation has extended over a considerable period of time which I think any reasonable person would consider an unreasonable length of time. While there may be many outstanding difficulties and perplexing ramifications involved in some of these cases, I think a hardship is worked upon a businessman who has all the responsibility of running a business, paying his bills and collecting from customers when his books and records are taken from him and kept by the department for many months in some cases. I think this is too severe a penalty to impose on a man despite the fact that he may be suspected of fraud or misrepresentation. Although it may mean more expense for the department, I think there is much to be said for either having a photostatic copy made of the books and records or expediting the investigation so that the documents are returned within a shorter period of time in order that the businessman may conduct his business in the ordinary way.
I do not think I would have risen to speak on this occasion if it were not for what I consider the totally unfounded remarks made by the hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska (Mr. Van Horne) which I believe are completely false.

Concerning the resolution
before the house the question arises as to whether we feel that certain work can be carried out by departmental officials. I recall when the estimates of the department with which the resolution before us deals were before the estimates committee last year the departmental officials were careful to point out that the backlog of work was caught up and they were now in a position to deal with the returns on a current basis. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the resolution submitted today merely accepts the representation of the department and puts their word to the test.
We all know that, when we pay our ordinary bills and receive a receipt from the person to whom the account is paid, the account is considered closed. It would seem to me that the law applying to individuals in this country should also apply to the government of the country. When we legislate for the individual we should say that the government are also bound by the same terms.
It was also pointed out in the estimates committee last year that the assessors of the Department of National Revenue bear no responsibility for advising a taxpayer if he has made a mistake in failing to claim certain exemptions. The officials of the department check the returns for mathematical errors to ascertain that the taxpayer has paid everything that is due to the department but they do not feel bound to advise him if he has failed to claim deductions to which he might

be fully entitled. Again this is a principle which does not apply to the ordinary individual. If through an error you overpay a person the law prescribes that you are entitled to receive back the amount you overpaid, but apparently that same law does not apply to the income tax department. If you overpay the department through an error they feel under no obligation to advise you as to the amount of overpayment and it is not remitted to you.
I completely support this resolution and I add my remarks to those of the hon. member who said that the parliamentary assistant's representations today do not speak very well for the other Liberal propaganda concerning the high standard of living which this country is enjoying. In the figures concerning the number of taxable returns submitted by the parliamentary assistant there was an admission of the very high percentage of people who do not make sufficient money to actually qualify as taxpayers. In other words they are not making the minimum amount of money which has been established as the basis below which you are not making enough to properly exist and should therefore not be called upon to pay income tax. The figures used by the parliamentary assistant in support of his department could be used equally well as a direct denial of the propaganda which the government has been spreading for the last few years concerning how well off everyone is in this country. The parliamentary assistant also admitted today that those earning $10,000 or less constitute 90 per cent of the Canadian people.
Ten per cent of the people of the country are making most of the money. According to the parliamentary assistant it would appear that the policy of the government is to permit the wealth of the country to be controlled by 10 per cent of the people. I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is smiling.

subsubtopic: FINAL RECEIPTS FOR THOSE WITH INCOMES OF $10,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take up very much time. I was beginning to feel that we were getting a long way from what was intended by the mover of the resolution. Sometimes when you get off the track it results in some of the statements that are made being given a wrong interpretation. I am prepared to support this resolution in the terms in which it appears on the order paper.
I think the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) put his finger on a very important point when he referred to public relations. I doubt if any hon. members can go beyond their own constituencies in speaking of a matter of this kind; I know I cannot. My experience has been that most people are honest and do not mind paying a fair amount of taxes. The complaints that come to me mostly concern people who have made their returns and who feel that things have therefore been wound up. Actually there is no limit on the winding up of these tax matters.
An amendment was approved last year reducing the period from six to four years, but that does not mean very much. Rightly or wrongly it happens quite often that an assessor will come along to a farmer and the minute he announces himself-most of these people are honest-the farmer wonders why he has come to see him and he gets excited. We all know that bad propaganda spreads very fast, and while I admit that this does not happen in all cases there have been cases where people have thought a settlement had been reached but after two or three years the matter is opened up again. In my constituency the assessors have done a fairly reasonably good job, but these matters do create unsatisfactory feelings. It makes the people begin to think that they are all crooks.
Some income tax officials will bend over backwards in order to try to help straighten out matters when approached in the right way, but they cannot go beyond the law and the regulations. When a person disagrees with an assessment made by a tax assessor his only course is to appeal. I am told that in many cases relief is given, but there are many appeals on the agenda. In order to start an appeal a man must put up security and then he has to wait anywhere from one to two or three years before his case is heard because there is such a backlog of appeals to be heard. When the amount involved is only $500 or $1,000 a man may feel that he just cannot afford to appeal his case. He has to have accountants. And, Mr. Speaker, there are many little transactions among farmers

Income Tax Act
which should never be taken into consideration; they do not amount to a hill of beans. However, once the department gets interested in a case it seems to pile up these little things to an extent that amazes the farmer. The farmer becomes excited; he "gets mad" and immediately suspects the department of "trying to do him." The quickest and easiest way of getting out of the problem is the course he will take, and I am satisfied that a good many people who have to pay $300, or $500 or maybe $1,000 would not have to pay at all if they could get their case to an appeal board within a reasonable time and at a reasonable expense.
That is the way I feel about it and for that reason I consider that this resolution will serve a very useful purpose if it enables the government to consider and reconsider some of these matters. I note that the effect of this resolution is limited to those whose incomes do not exceed $10,000, and I feel that this being the case the government would probably not lose much money anyway, even supposing there were to be some mistakes. The parliamentary assistant to the minister has led us to believe that this taxpaying group is the largest in the country, and if this is so I believe it is time more information was made available regarding it. The figure of $10,000 is, maybe, too high a figure to have specified; it would be interesting to have the views of the department upon a possible alternative figure. But I do think there is a class of people who should be given a final receipt at the end of two years-

speechtext:
When I read this resolution over, Mr. Speaker, I was in very much the position of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny)-I felt I would like some clarification of what period really is meant. I note that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) does not agree with the impression of the mover of this resolution; also, the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Montgomery) has indicated his interpretation of this as meaning "two years". From my own point of view I can understand that there may be some confusion as to the real essence of what is contained in this motion.
One other thing. I think this motion, if it were accepted, would create two classes of taxpayers in Canada. The motion as now worded affects those whose income amounts to $10,000 a year or less. In the 1954 taxation statistics it was shown there were 3,125,100 individual taxpayers; there were fewer than 60,000 taxpayers whose annual income exceeded $10,000. Now, if it were possible for the mover of this motion to accept the suggestion of his colleague from Greenwood that the time limit be extended to two years-[DOT] and certainly there has been evidence on the part of the government of willingness to close the gap, because only last year it was brought down from six years to four years-some progress might be made. As we note, there is not quite complete agreement at the present time between the mover of the resolution, on the one hand, and the hon. member for Greenwood on the other, and I think we might almost indicate that all individual taxpayers be included in this resolution, in which case we would not be making any distinction.
I have read this resolution over with a great deal of concern because the mover of this resolution is within the same tax office as I am myself. Two or three things were said here this afternoon which I think cast a reflection on all income tax offices. The words "reaching out to control private lives" were used; the words "fill their pockets" were also used. I hope that at no time I will ever be accused of trying to use catch phrases that will leave an aspersion upon those people who are engaged to do a type of job which is not, I am sure, the easiest work to do.
One other thing. The mover of this motion was reading a number of supporting resolutions from different counties, but I note that he did not mention the county from which I come. I do not know whether they did not

support this resolution of a year ago. However, I am of the opinion that something needs to be done, because only this weekend I had a taxpayer at my home whose case is being investigated back to 1942. It is almost impossible for this individual to get all the receipts that are necessary if he is to prove his case. The original assessment was for some $28,000 but after he was able to establish a certain number of receipts, a second assessment of $22,000 was made. Then, after a great deal of effort he secured more receipts, and the third assessment was for $10,000 plus about $3,600 in penalties. During all this time he had been employing an accountant, and I can readily understand why he engaged an accountant after hearing the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that lawyers were not very good on this type of case. But this has proved an expensive procedure for this taxpayer to have to follow, and the money he has to pay in defending his case is money that cannot be charged as an expense. While I agree, Mr. Speaker, that this may be departing from the subject a little, I think this is one question which should possibly be considered when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is reviewing the tax structure.
So, Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to indicate my interest in this resolution as brought forward by the hon. member for Middlesex East.

Mr. Speaker, there is just one point I would like to emphasize-the point made by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) when he said that the Income Tax Department could have much better public relations than it has, and that they should be considered as more friendly to the people whose affairs they have to investigate than they are. I had a personal experience. I may say that I have no personal axe to grind with the income tax department. This happened in 1947. One week end when I arrived home I found a form letter addressed to me and stating that I owed the income tax department a considerable sum of money for the previous year's taxes. Mr. Speaker, if I had had a weak heart at that time, I would not be here to tell you about the matter. I can tell you that I nearly fell through the floor. I did not know where I could dig up this money. I felt that there had been an error but I was not too sure. The accountant who looked after my affairs was away for the week end and I was forced to decide to let the matter go until the next week end. I may say that the department gave me only a few days in which to pay up, or else. However, when I arrived home next week end, I found a letter from the income tax department stating 82715-46
Income Tax Act
that they were sorry, that they had made a mistake, that they had found my cheque in their files and just to ignore their letter of such and such a date.
Mr. Speaker, I do not object to mistakes. We all make them. But this was merely a sort of slaphappy way of making an apology for a mistake that was made by them. Some person should really have come out to see me personally and to apologize for this mistake. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that if I had had a weak heart, as I said before, I would have dropped right there and that is just one instance. From some of the gestapo methods that are being employed today in some parts of the country, I know that is just what should happen. The public relations in connection with income tax should certainly be improved in no uncertain way.

I will let it go at that, then. Previously I did not have time in which to go into the taxation statistics for the year 1956 but I am going to take a moment or two now to do so. According to the report of 1956-that would be for the 1955 taxation year-I find that some 3,341,490 people in Canada had incomes under $10,000. I said also that the income tax department employed something over 6,000 people. I find that means there was one employee for every 500 taxpayers. It does not appear to me as though the problem would be insurmountable.
Coming back to what the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa had to say about public relations, I may say that we have municipal tax collectors and I have never heard of a case of animosity towards municipal tax collectors in which the affairs of the taxpayer had been handled in such a manner that any blame was attached to them. However, such is not the case in the income tax department. I think the hon. member made a very good suggestion. Probably the department will recognize it and take steps to correct the matter.
Mention was made by the parliamentary assistant that probably I represent a rural constituency. It is true that in years gone by Middlesex East was a rural constituency, but today approximately five out of six people are residents in the city of London. This is the bundle of letters I have received in the last year or year and a half and with the exception of about 10 they are all from business and professional people. Farmers are not inclined to write letters. They will come to see you, but they do not put their troubles in writing. Business and professional people are used to writing letters and consequently one receives more from them.
This motion may be defeated in the house, Mr. Speaker, but I feel certain from the nature

of the discussion on both sides that the presentation of it will have a good effect. I believe I have answered all the questions that were asked and I hope those who feel there is some merit in the motion will support it.

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of taking steps to relieve the financial crisis in education, without encroaching in any way on the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in this field, by granting financial assistance to the various provinces for the expansion and equalization of educational opportunity across Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I bring forward this resolution, and the house no doubt knows that it is not for the first time. I regret very much that there may not be the time before the house rises tonight to give the matter a thorough discussion, but such time as there is we can profitably spend on it. I bring the resolution forward not for political reasons, not with any geographical bias, but simply because I believe the implementation of this resolution would be a good thing for the children of Canada.
When I refer to the children of Canada may I say, although it may be used against me at a later date-that is immaterial to me-that I am no more concerned with the interests of the children of my own province of Saskatchewan than I am with the interests of the children of Nova Scotia, Quebec, Manitoba or any other Canadian province. The resolution has as its object the establishment of some degree of equalization of educational opportunity for all Canadian children.
Such equality of opportunity is surely the birthright of every Canadian child. The present state of inequality of opportunity in education across Canada is due simply to the lack of adequate finances and the differences in the ability of the various provinces to assist education from their own resources; therefore the resolution suggests that the

Education
federal government should financially support the provinces in such educational efforts as they are now putting forth or which they might decide to inaugurate. The program of education, the subjects taught and the administration of the educational assistance must lie in the hands of the provinces themselves; with that I am in complete agreement. For that reason I have been careful to write into the resolution the following words:
.	.	. without encroaching in any way on the
exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in this field.
In opposing this resolution in former times when it was discussed the question of such aid not being constitutional was the only argument the government was able or found expedient to produce. Usually early in the debate the government put up a cabinet minister, a sort of government hatchet man, who had the double function of using one end of the hatchet, perhaps the blade end, on the content of the resolution itself, while the handle served as a kind of pointer which enabled the backbenchers on the Liberal side to know in which direction they must go.
I think on one occasion the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) led the brigade, in spite of the fact that the premier of his own Liberal province of Manitoba has frequently asked for federal aid for education. On another occasion the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) led the Liberal troops into battle, in spite of the fact that at the very time which he launched his attack the educational expenditure per child in his own province of Newfoundland was $86 as compared with $292 in the province of the minister who sits beside him, British Columbia.
The aforesaid members of the government have faithfully followed the line set by the cabinet ministers, though to my personal knowledge they have followed with increasing reluctance as the years have gone by. One can understand what pressures must be placed on those members who oppose this resolution, particularly in some of the more needy provinces. 1 am thinking particularly of the maritimes, for I cannot understand how any member representing a constituency in one of the Atlantic provinces could be conscientiously opposed to this particular resolution. However, as I said in a speech the other day, I think we are making progress.
When I came to this house 12 years ago and raised this question of federal aid to education there was a polite, or perhaps not so polite, raising of eyebrows. "What?" they said. "Do we mention education in the federal parliament? This is solely a matter of provincial jurisdiction". But we in this house have

come to accept federal grants to various forms of education. We have accepted, and gratefully as far as I am concerned, federal grants for technical education, vocational education, grants to universities, and the very successful D.V.A. plan upon which I compliment the government. Can anyone say conscientiously that the acceptance of those particular grants has in any way involved federal control, or has in any way interfered with the jurisdiction of the provinces in the matter of education?
And what of the present? The people of the United States have a special day or week devoted to practically every subject you can name, and I suppose we tend to imitate them. I know there is such a thing as an education week, and I am going to suggest that in this House of Commons we have had "education week" during the past week at the end of which I speak. Not only do we have the grants I have mentioned, but we have had foreshadowed legislation which is to increase grants for technical education and vocational education, increased grants to universities, the setting up of a Canada Council which is to administer some of those grants and to promote increased expenditures in the arts and sciences, and to administer increased scholarships with emphasis upon the humanities.
What a change has taken place over the years I have been in this house. Those who have conscientiously and persistently advocated these changes might like to take unto themselves some credit for the fact that we have made some advances in this field, but I would suggest that although perhaps we have had some success in popularizing and publicizing the need for federal aid to education, it has been hard economic facts which have in large part produced the change. There is the dilemma in which the municipalities find themselves, the increasing difficulty they experience in carrying on adequate educational services. I think they feel almost unanimously that the basis for taxation for the purposes of education must be broadened in some way or other. No longer can it be put on the uncertain basis of real estate in the local field, as it has been in the past, with the assistance of the provinces which in many cases have not been able to give assistance in full measure. Speaking nationally, there is the growing national consciousness that other nations, some of them opposed to us ideologically, have been forging ahead in these matters while we have been indulging in the niceties of constitutional argument.
I have been encouraged by what I detect as a change in attitude in this house. I have

reason to congratulate the hon. member lor Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). I cannot quote his speech because it was made in another debate, but since it was similar in subject to the present debate I think I can at least refer to it. He was even vociferous in his acceptance of increased grants for technical and vocational training. Those things having been settled, he then turned to the problem in the lower schools and said there was a gap left that must be filled. He did not suggest it had to be filled by federal funds-he has to remember his position-but having made the proper genuflection to the constitution he proceeded to say what this gap was, and it was the need for assistance to secondary and primary schools in his particular district.
What was the solution he offered? I might almost have put the words into his mouth. The solution he offered was that the provinces would have to be urged to give education a great share of the grants which they receive from the federal government.
After all, is that not largely what I have been advocating in this house for years? The hon. member felt, as did another Liberal hon. member, that this should be handled in a delicate way. I appreciate the need on his part for such delicate handling.
I also wish to offer my congratulations to another hon. member of this house who made a very useful and eloquent speech. I realize that he was talking about university grants, another field of education, but he supported the same general principles. He said that every Canadian, no matter what his background or province or racial origin, should benefit equally in the field of education and other fields. He said that was the aim of the government to which he pays allegiance in the making of such grants. He said also that the sooner we placed educational facilities within reach of a greater number of young Canadians, the better it would be for the whole country.
As I said, that might have been an echo of my own voice. In his eloquent speech this member, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) said he was in warm support of the type of education we were discussing at that time. The hon. member did bring in the constitutional angle and said he would be loath to do anything that was against the constitution. I wish he would rise today and in that same eloquent way support the resolution I have moved. If he did so he would find himself in good company. In a speech such as I am about to make I cannot bring in too much documentation. I have files a foot thick containing everything that
Education
everybody has said with regard to this subject over the last dozen years. I have resolutions which have been passed by the Canadian school trustees' association, the Canadian teachers' federation, boards of trade, Legion branches, town councils and, as recently as the last two or three days, the Canadian Labour Congress. The Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour presented a brief to the government the other day in favour of university grants.
There are those who would argue that such grants are unconstitutional in terms of the British North America Act. Mr. Picard, the president of that organization, made no bones about his position on these grants. Last Friday evening he was interviewed as part of a news broadcast, and said that in his opinion anyone who was against these university grants would be against old age pensions and family allowances. I have made this same statement in regard to the matter I am talking about today. It would seem that perhaps my case is making some progress.
I have also asked, what about health? I do not think the word "health" is mentioned in the British North America Act; the Minister of Justice can correct me if I am wrong. However, we have grants in aid of health education. We have grants to assist the provinces in the building of hospitals. I do not think anyone has ever raised any question as to their constitutionality. There are other reasons, I suppose.
There is one organization which has made a special contribution to the cause of education, the Canadian school trustees' association. Naturally we would expect that that would be so. I believe it was in 1953 that this association formed a research committee to look into the whole subject of education financing in Canada. This is the book to which I had reference, and I would recommend its reading to any hon. member who is interested at all in this problem. It is entitled "School Finance in Canada" and was published in 1955. It is the report of the Canadian school trustees' association school finance research committee. The man responsible for the organization of this work was Dr. M. E. LaZerte, who is well known to educationists across this country.
When the Canadian school trustees' association had completed this book and had arrived at certain conclusions in regard to the whole matter they decided to interview the cabinet, particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in order to plead their case. Whatever his reasons may have been, whether political or constitutional, I think it was unfortunate that the Prime Minister should have refused to receive those gentlemen who came to see him on that particular

Education
occasion. Let us give the Prime Minister credit for being honest when he said that since he considered this matter was not within the purview of the federal government he had to refuse to see the representatives of this influential and widespread organization. I think in more than one way that action was a mistake. That is a serious charge for me to bring, so perhaps I had better document it. I have here an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of May 24, 1956, reading as follows:
In a recently prepared brief, the Canadian school trustees' association thanked Canada's Prime Minister and cabinet for granting an interview. But the trustees were too optimistic. They had to add a postscript: "Unfortunately the Prime Minister refused to hear the delegation". On parliament hill, it seems, scant recognition is given to any national interest in the well-being of the provincial school systems.
Yet this brief presents powerful arguments for federal aid to education-arguments that cannot be ignored.
May I interject to say that I intend to let this editorial make my argument for me at the moment.
It points out that the kind and quality of education provided in the provinces are of direct concern to Canada's civil service and its armed forces, its economic development and its trade. It states that tens of thousands of teachers have very little academic or professional training, and declares that "without federal assistance it is impossible to staff the schools of all provinces with adequately trained teachers." For the next ten years, about $200 million annually will have to be spent on new schools and renovations. The trustees contend that revenues-federal revenues-from income and corporation taxes, sales taxes and customs duties, should pay part of the cost.
The trustees' brief quotes Dr. Garnet Page, general manager of the chemical institute of Canada-
-as warning that as a matter of survival Canada must train more mathematics and science teachers and produce more scientists and technicians. It quotes pleas for federal aid from the Canadian teachers' federation, the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, a royal commission on New Brunswick's schools and the premier of Manitoba, and it adds its own plea.
It is hardly possible to maintain that these representations are not of national concern. If parliament should decide that it ought to give greater aid to education-on the basis, incidentally, of ample precedents like existing vocational training assistance and research scholarships-it could surely find means that would involve no interference with provincial control of the schools.
I shall proceed in my own words from here. I did mention this book "School Finance in Canada" put out by the Canadian school trustees' association, and I would like to have the permission of the house to put on the record in the form of four columns a sample of the type of research that has been done there. What I have brought down here are four tables, showing respectively the cost of primary and secondary education per pupil in each province; persons teaching without professional training; the percentage of enrolled grade 7 students reaching grade 11, and the percentage of population aged 15 to 19 not attending any school. That is not the way in which this was drawn up originally, but I have chosen these columns as a sample of the work which was carried out.
If you, sir, could secure me the permission of the house to have these placed on the record-
